Building Bridge

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Move a bridge across a river so the road from one town to the other is as short as you can make it.
How to play: Drag a town or the bridge dot with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Press Snap to shortest to see the best spot.
Look for the math

Moving the bridge changes two slanted road pieces but not the river crossing: the bridge is always the same length. So the puzzle is really about making just the two land pieces as short as possible. There is a neat way to turn that into one straight line.

Slide one town across the river

Let the bridge go from C on the upper bank to C' straight below it on the lower bank. The translation that takes C to C' also takes B to B'. It moves every point the same distance in the same direction, so it keeps lengths: C B' = C' B. That is why the land part of the road, AC + C'B, can be written as AC + CB'. The river crossing adds the same fixed width to every route, so whichever choice makes the land part shortest makes the whole road shortest.

A straight line beats a bent one

Now A is above the upper bank and B' is below it. For any point C on that bank, the triangle inequality gives AC + CB' ≥ AB', with equality only when C lies on the straight segment from A to B'. So the best bridge is exactly where the line AB' crosses the upper bank. Its total length is AB' + river width.

The other translation gives the same answer

The old article also says you can slide A across the river to A' instead and draw A'B. Its meeting point with the lower bank is C', directly below the first bridge spot. The logic test checks both crossings against the applet's own line-intersection calculation on hundreds of town positions and river widths: the two points are the same bridge, and the two ways give the same minimum length. The dashed lines on the page are that very construction.

Try hiding the hint lines, find the best bridge by dragging, then press Snap to shortest to check your eye. The original Java applet chose its towns at random; this page starts from one fixed picture so two runs can be compared.
